stem: A client is receiving Droplet Precautions for a respiratory infection. How should the nurse determine when the Transmission-Based Precautions can be discontinued?

options.A: Continue Droplet Precautions indefinitely because pathogen-specific stopping criteria do not exist.
options.B: Stop Droplet Precautions exactly 24 hours after they begin for every respiratory infection, regardless of the diagnosis or clinical course.
options.C: Use the organism- and condition-specific duration criteria in current infection-control guidance, because precautions continue while transmission risk persists and the required duration varies by infection.
options.D: Discontinue precautions whenever the client requests it, regardless of transmission risk, treatment status, or infection-control guidance.

rationale: CDC states that Transmission-Based Precautions remain in effect while risk for transmission persists and that the duration depends on the infectious agent and condition. Appendix A gives pathogen-specific durations—for example, some Droplet Precautions continue until 24 hours after effective therapy, whereas others continue for the duration of illness or according to other criteria. Therefore C is correct. A, B, and D incorrectly apply an indefinite, universal 24-hour, or preference-based rule.
educational_objective: Use pathogen- and condition-specific CDC criteria to determine the duration of Transmission-Based Precautions rather than applying a universal stopping time.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Guideline for Isolation Precautions — III. Precautions to Prevent Transmission of Infectious Agents; Appendix A: Type and Duration of Precautions Recommended for Selected Infections and Conditions
source_version_date: Appendix A page February 7, 2025; current CDC guidance accessed 2026-08-16

source_claim_supported: Transmission-Based Precautions continue while transmission risk persists, and duration varies by pathogen/condition according to current CDC guidance.

source_original.stem: A client is on droplet precautions for a respiratory infection. How is the duration of transmission-based precautions determined?

options.A: Continue every droplet precaution indefinitely because pathogen-specific stopping criteria do not exist
options.B: Stop every droplet precaution exactly 24 hours after it begins regardless of diagnosis or symptoms
options.C: Use organism- and condition-specific criteria while the transmission risk persists, following current guidance
options.D: Discontinue precautions whenever the client requests it, independent of transmission risk or guidance

source_original.rationale: CDC states that Transmission-Based Precautions remain in effect while transmission risk persists, with duration depending on the pathogen, clinical course, testing, treatment, and applicable facility or public-health guidance.
source_original.source_detail: Type and Duration of Precautions Recommended for Selected Infections and Conditions; updated Feb. 7, 2025; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Preserved the correct organism-specific duration principle, added the CDC transmission-risk rule and examples without imposing a universal timeframe, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: CDC Isolation Precautions guidance; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: CDC Appendix A dated 2025-02-07 with current update history; rechecked 2026-08-16.
audit_findings.claim_audit: CDC directly states precautions remain while transmission risk persists and Appendix A supplies pathogen-specific duration criteria.

distractor_audit.B: False; 24 hours applies to some conditions, not all Droplet Precautions.
distractor_audit.D: Client preference does not supersede transmission-risk criteria.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C reflects the general CDC rule without overgeneralizing a disease-specific duration.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are duration rules; the key depends on infection-control knowledge.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN p.8 explicitly includes infection-prevention principles and education.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read CDC general duration text and Appendix A examples, specifically challenged whether a universal 24-hour rule could ever fit the broad stem, and confirmed C remained uniquely correct.
